intuition.text: Pip is a survey rover beside a hot test beacon. An escape instruction tells its motor which way to accelerate; it does not teleport Pip away or erase motion already heading inwards. Watch the velocity arrow as well as the outward push.
intuition.situation: Use this response when Pip should open a gap from a known point. This study runs the scene engine’s Flee: its push fades with distance, so the example also shows the boundary between asking for escape and deciding how motion should stop.

example.name: Pip leaves the test beacon
example.description: Pip starts at {start} on an open line, with the beacon fixed at {threat} and initial velocity {initialVelocity} units/s. Its motor allows {maxAcceleration} units/s² and {maxSpeed} units/s. Updates are {timeStep} s apart over a {duration} s window. The scene engine fixes its flee radius at {engineRadius} units; that is an engine choice, not a universal safe distance.

steps.title: Find the direction away
steps.text: Subtract the beacon’s position from Pip’s: the signed displacement is {offset} and its magnitude is {distance} units. Normalising this displacement chooses away. At exact coincidence the displacement supplies no direction, so this engine returns no push.

steps.title: Ask the engine for its fading push
steps.text: Call scene-engine flee on the current body and beacon. Inside its fixed {engineRadius}-unit radius it scales the away direction by maxAcceleration times the remaining fraction of the radius. Here the fade is {fade} and the signed acceleration is {acceleration} units/s². At or beyond the radius the output is zero. This differs from a constant maximum-acceleration Flee.

steps.title: Let the motor change velocity
steps.text: Multiply the acceleration by {timeStep} s and add it to velocity, then enforce the {maxSpeed} units/s speed limit. Acceleration changes motion over time: an inward-moving Pip can continue towards the beacon while the outward push brakes it.

steps.title: Move with the new velocity
steps.text: Advance position using that updated velocity. The next position is {nextPosition} units. This study-local open-line motor keeps existing velocity when Flee becomes silent; it adds neither a stop at the circle nor the full scene’s other steering rules.

pseudocode.ordinary:
offset = position - threat
distance = abs(offset)
body = bodyAt(position, velocity, maxSpeed, maxAcceleration)

acceleration = sceneEngine.flee(body, point(threat))
// engine: normalise(offset) * maxAcceleration * max(0, 1 - distance / engineRadius)
// normalise(0) is 0

velocity = clamp(velocity + acceleration * timeStep,
                 -maxSpeed, maxSpeed)

position = position + velocity * timeStep

visual.textEquivalent: At {seconds} s, Pip is at {position}, {distance} units from the beacon at {threat}, with velocity {velocity} units/s and acceleration {acceleration} units/s²; the circle marks the {engineRadius}-unit response radius and {motionState}.

implementations.relevance: gdx-ai is a Java game-AI library with steering behaviours over either planar or spatial vectors. Its Flee class is a small reusable implementation of repulsion from a target position.
implementations.explanation: Flee extends Seek and reverses the position subtraction. It normalises the resulting vector, scales it to the configured maximum linear acceleration and sets angular acceleration to zero. The class returns a steering output for game code to apply; this method contains no distance fade or stopping rule.

references.title: AI for Games, third edition · Chapter 3 Movement, §3.3.3 Seek and Flee
references.supports: The book covers Flee in Chapter 3 Movement, section 3.3.3 Seek and Flee.

references.title: gdx-ai 1.8.2 · Flee.java
references.supports: A public implementation reverses the position displacement, normalises it and applies the configured maximum linear acceleration without a distance fade in that method.

limits: With Pip exactly on the beacon and initially still, the away vector is zero. The comparison changes only starting position and leaves Pip stuck; choosing an escape direction needs another rule.
An outward acceleration does not immediately reverse an inward velocity. Pip can move closer before the motor has removed that approach speed.
Leaving the response circle means the push is silent, not that Pip has stopped or reached a safe destination. This motor coasts; a complete game must decide what follows the escape instruction.
The example has an open line and a fixed beacon. The rule reads neither obstacles nor a moving threat’s future position, so it cannot select a route around a barrier or anticipate an interception.

nearby.why: Reach for Seek when Pip should close the displacement towards a point instead of opening it.
Reach for Evade when the threatening actor moves and its predicted position matters to the escape.
Reach for Separation when Pip must part from several neighbours rather than repel one named point.
Reach for Obstacle and wall avoidance when a direct outward push can lead into a barrier.
